sources.text: Ignition, flame growth, spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flow, including reduced-oxygen runs (initial O2 13.6–22.2 % vol). Data feed the combustion models used to design detection and suppression systems.

sources.title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator — approach
sources.text: In addition to the flight experiments, in normal gravity testing will continue. These tests will involve gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels. These experiments will further establish the validation of the BRE for 1-g applications and show its usefulness to establish 1-g ignition and extinction limits. As available, drop facility testing will be used to refine procedures, test instrumentation, and help to establish viable flow conditions.

sources.title: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography — objective
sources.text: To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.

sources.title: BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids — insight:bass-1g-screening-gap
sources.text: 1-g material screening is not automatically conservative. Spacecraft material selection relies on NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, which ranks materials by 1-g behaviour. BASS and BASS-II were built on the hypothesis that, with adequate ventilation, materials burn as well if not better in microgravity than in normal gravity. Which flow speeds and flow directions must a microgravity-relevant material test include?

sources.title: SAFFIRE-II — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II — approach
sources.text: Depending on the sample material, the Saffire-II was conducted at an air flow velocity of either 20 or 30 cm/s, the flow being either concurrent or opposed. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked. Details related to samples and experimental parameters are provided in the Experimental Details file in the Science document folder.

sources.title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator — hypothesis
sources.text: The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix). Thus achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than a candle flame, this has not been shown before.

sources.title: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography — approach
sources.text: The approach combined high-resolution computational modeling with experimental validation to study concurrent flame spread in microgravity. A previously developed computational framework was employed to run fully coupled simulations of fluid–solid responses, focusing on materials subject to charring and ablation. Within this framework, the unsteady FGM method was implemented and tested on various BASS geometries, including flat sheets, spheres, and rod-shaped polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) samples, as well as wax cylinders.

sources.title: BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2
sources.text: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations are free text; flow units to be confirmed in the BASS-II documentation; flame-spread rates are in the raw video data.

sources.title: More oxygen: droplet flames more often survive to burnout
sources.text: FLEX droplet tests in N2-only atmospheres that ended in flame extinction before burnout — Heptane: 5/17 at 21 % O2 vs 0/11 at 30–34 % O2; Methanol: 9/12 at 21 % O2 vs 2/13 at 30–34 % O2. Remaining tests ended in burnout ('completion') or droplet disruption. Limitation: Isolated droplets, two fuels; 'extinction' here means the flame went out before the droplet was consumed (often radiative), not the action of an extinguisher. Counts, not a model.

sources.title: Microgravity and 1-g rankings of materials can disagree
sources.text: In SAFFIRE-II, 4 of 4 silicone samples (0.27–1.03 mm) had a burn length of about 0 in microgravity at 20 cm/s, while 2 of the 4 matching 1-g reference burns were complete. Flames did spread in microgravity over: PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric). Limitation: One test per configuration; single flow speed and near-normal O2.

sources.title: Stopping ventilation may not be enough in oxygen-enriched cabins
sources.text: In quiescent microgravity, BRE flames emulating condensed materials (e.g. PMMA, nylon) kept burning quasi-steadily in the elevated-oxygen atmospheres considered for future spacecraft, whereas comparable flames at 21 % O2 self-extinguished in a short time. PSI describes these results as preliminary. Limitation: Gaseous emulation of solids; per-test pressure not in the summary table; results flagged preliminary.

top_passage.text: A basic understanding of cool flames is important for understanding ignition phenomena of practical fuels and fuel additives. Cool flames play a key role in the development and selection of new fuels and the design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines. The research will also help combustion chemists to develop new computational models to compute combustion performance in for many practical applications on earth, including an understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines.

top_passage.text: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing). The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion. The combustion of fossil fuel is the primary human source of greenhouse gas and acid rain and furthermore creates soot, which can be beneficial but is also a health hazard. Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions.

top_passage.text: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity.
